newsitem.title: CANADA: Tax cheating widespread in Canada, study says.
newsitem.headline: Tax cheating widespread in Canada, study says.

text.p: Inequities in Canada's tax system are encouraging widespread tax evasion and driving many Canadians into the underground economy, a study released on Wednesday by a right-leaning research institute said.
The Vancouver-based Fraser Institute said that Canada's underground economy could be as much as 20 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), or almost C$160 billion.
The institute based its finding on an historical analysis of the cash circulating in the Canadian economy.

The institute's figure is in sharp contrast to Canadian government statistics putting the underground economy at 2.7 to 5.0 percent of GDP. The government, however, does not include untaxed illegal earnings as part of its definition of the underground economy.
The institute said that the Goods and Services Tax, a federal value-added tax introduced in 1991, was the most important factor contributing to the growth of the underground economy.
"The underground economy is growing by stealth in Canada," said Peter Spiro, an economist and contributing author for the institute.
Spiro said the underground economy grew by C$14 billion between 1991 and 1993, which translated into a C$6 billion revenue loss for all levels of government in Canada.

The study reported that 74 percent of Canadians surveyed agreed that the tax system was basically unfair to average Canadians. Sixty-one percent said there was a good or fair amount of tax evasion in Canada.
The study said that such attitudes toward taxation influenced Canadians to earn untaxed income in the underground economy.

"The tragedy of the enormous growth of the underground economy is that once the domain of drug pushers and bootleggers, it is increasingly frequented by otherwise law-abiding citizens," said Michael Walker, the institute's executive director.
